text:
LLMs that can skim their context to selectively read the tokens that matter.

Skimming beats full reads: up to 11x speedup & 3x lower memory for long-context prefill.

Paper · Quick start · How it works · Reproducing results

## ⚡ What is TokenGate? Current language models read all tokens of their input context, processing each one through all model layers. **TokenGated Language Models can *skim*, selectively processing only context that matters** through learned token selection for up to **11.3x faster** prefill with **3.4x lower memory** at **no accuracy degradation**. TokenGate extends existing models to enable conditional computing, akin to MoE layers, but for a different scaling dimension: long-context inputs. ## 🔥 Make your LLM a Token-Gated Language Model TokenGate is **a drop-in neural network component that extends existing trained models** (e.g., trained transformers or hybrid architectures) to enable learnable token selection with light-weight adaptation. You can **adapt your model with TokenGate as a replacement to standard fine-tuning or PEFT**. While standard fine-tuning allows models to improve task-specific accuracy, training models with TokenGate allows models to *improve both accuracy and prefill efficiency* for Pareto-optimal inference performance. Training with TokenGate is as simple and efficient as standard PEFT training.

## 📦 Installation ```bash uv venv && uv pip install -e . # Python ≥ 3.10, CUDA PyTorch ≥ 2.9; ".[train]" for training ``` Recommended: `python kernels/fa2bias/build.py` builds the fast FlashAttention-2 key-bias kernel that the dense-Qwen3 defaults use (needs `nvcc`). Everything also runs without it via FlexAttention: inference falls back automatically with a warning; training asks for an explicit `attn_backend="flex". ## 🚀 Quick start ### Inference If you're already familiar with 🤗 transformers (`from_pretrained` / `apply_chat_template` / `generate`), getting started with TokenGate will be a breeze. Two things are new: a `{state}` placeholder marks the prunable document in your context, and `generate` takes a keep-budget `max_kept_prefill_tokens` — the number of state tokens that are retained for full processing during prefill. The example below loads the released needle-in-a-haystack checkpoint and answers a question about one fact planted in ~32,000 tokens of essays. The sample haystack ships with the repo, so it runs as-is: ```python import json from transformers import AutoTokenizer from tokengate import load_model, apply_chat_template # one object: base model + gate + paired adapter; gate layer and base model # are read from the checkpoint's own metadata model = load_model("liana313/tokengate-niah-qwen3-1.7b") tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model.base_model) # ~32k tokens of essays with one planted fact about San Francisco essays = json.loads(next(open("examples/data/niah_32k_samples.jsonl")))["body"] prompt = ("Answer the question using only the document below. " "Keep your answer short and direct.\n\n" "Question: What is the best thing to do in San Francisco?\n\n" "Document:\n{state}\n\nAnswer:") ids = apply_chat_template(tok, prompt, state=essays) for k in (None, 2000, 500, 100): # None = keep every state token out = model.generate([ids], tok, max_kept_prefill_tokens=k) print(k, f"{out.prefill_s * 1e3:5.0f} ms", out.answers[0]) # K prefill answer # all 1471 ms eat a sandwich and sit in Dolores Park on a sunny day # 2000 153 ms eat a sandwich and sit in Dolores Park on a sunny day # 500 157 ms eat a sandwich and sit in Dolores Park on a sunny day # 100 130 ms eat a sandwich and sit in Dolores Park on a sunny day ``` One gate serves every K: the planted needle is still answered verbatim with 144 of 32,191 prompt tokens (0.4%) in the KV cache, at ~11× lower time-to-first-token. ### Training Training looks like a TRL/PEFT recipe: a config object plus a trainer that takes your dataset. The example below trains the same needle-in-a-haystack gate the inference example uses. First generate the synthetic haystacks: ```bash python datasets/niah_kamradt/generate_niah_kamradt.py --output-file niah.jsonl --n-train 12000 ``` Then train: ```python import json from tokengate import TokenGateConfig, TokenGateTrainer niah = [json.loads(l) for l in open("niah.jsonl")] rows = lambda split: [{"article": f"{r['body']}\n\nQuestion: {r['question']}", "answer": r["answer"]} for r in niah if r["split"] == split] config = TokenGateConfig( base_model="Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B", gate_layer=1, # layer L whose hidden states the gate scores output_dir="e2e_gates/niah-1p7b", learning_rate=1e-4, epochs=20, k_eval=[2000], # in-training eval K sweep # LoRA co-adaptation (the backbone itself stays frozen) lora_rank=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_lr=1e-4, lora_targets=["q_proj", "v_proj"], wandb_project="token-gate", # omit to disable logging ) trainer = TokenGateTrainer( config, train_dataset=rows("train"), # [{"article": ..., "answer": ...}, ...] eval_dataset=rows("test"), task="niah_kamradt", # registered prompt + metric (datasets/tasks) ) trainer.train() # → e2e_gates/niah-1p7b/gate_final.pt ``` Each row is `{"article": , "answer": }` (`"state"` is an alias for `"article"`; any HF Dataset with those columns works). The trainer tokenizes the rows, carves a deterministic eval split from `eval_dataset`, and launches a DDP `torchrun` run on all visible GPUs (`num_gpus` overrides), blocking until the final gate and its name-paired LoRA land in `output_dir`. Already-prepared data under `datasets/` can be passed by name instead — `train_dataset="biodex/biodex_reactions"` — and uses the store's own val split. The gate trains against randomly sampled keep-budgets, so one trained gate serves any K at inference. The Qwen3 defaults train on the key-bias kernel from [Installation](#-installation) and fail fast without it; set `attn_backend="flex"` to train on the no-build kernels (the Qwen3.5 hybrid defaults to flex, and other model families must set it explicitly). ## 🔍 How it works

A gate module at an early layer *L* scores every token of the prunable input (the **state**) and keeps the top-*K*. The layers above *L* process only those *K* tokens and store only their KV-cache entries — pruned tokens never consume compute or memory above the gate, which is where both the time-to-first-token and the peak-memory savings come from. Everything outside the `{state}` placeholder (instructions, the question, the generated answer) is never pruned. The top-*K* selection introduces a challenge for end-to-end training since top-*K is non-differentiable. To address this we introduce *Token-gated attention**, a mechanism which re-weights each kept token's attention logic using its token importance score, providing a gradient path for e2e training. The gate trains end-to-end with standard next-token prediction, jointly with the model backbone. ## 📊 Reproducing results ### Benchmark examples `examples/niah_demo.py` downloads the trained gate for Qwen3-1.7B (gate layer 1) from the Hub and runs the classic Kamradt needle-in-a-haystack on committed ~32k-token Paul Graham essay haystacks: for each keep-budget it reports retrieval accuracy, prefill time-to-first-token, and how much of the needle sentence itself survived the pruning: ```bash python examples/niah_demo.py # 5 haystacks, K = all/2000/500/100 python examples/niah_demo.py --k 500 --n 2 # one budget, fewer rows ``` Validated output (5 haystacks, needle depths 11–100%, one GPU): ``` kept tokens acc TTFT(ms) speedup needle kept ------------------------------------------------------ all 1.00 1533.6 1.00x 100% 2000 1.00 153.4 10.00x 100% 500 1.00 144.3 10.63x 100% 100 1.00 137.2 11.18x 100% ``` Every needle is retrieved at every budget — even keeping 100 of ~32k tokens, the gate's selection lands squarely on the needle sentence. A second demo on real data follows the same pattern: `examples/biodexr_demo.py` (BioDEX adverse-drug-reaction extraction; mean exact-match set F1 0.622 at K=2000 over the committed val articles). Both pipelines are covered by `python -m tokengate.e2e_gate.tests.test_niah_demo` and `...tests.test_biodexr_demo`, and `--gate-attn flex` avoids the custom-kernel build at some speed cost. For a full accuracy + latency comparison against standard prefill, `benchmarks/run_benchmark.py` measures, on the same samples and base model, **accuracy** (the task's own metric) and **TTFT** (prefill-to-first-token, batch size 1) for three arms: standard full prefill of the base model, TokenGate with nothing pruned (the accuracy reference), and TokenGate at each configured K. Each config in `benchmarks/configs/` (niah, repobench, biodexr) pairs a released checkpoint with the prepared dataset's pinned eval split — `--split val` is the 50-row in-training eval partition, `--split test` the full reserved held-out partition: ```bash python benchmarks/run_benchmark.py --config benchmarks/configs/niah.yaml --split test ``` Validated held-out **test** results (every reserved test row, batch 1, one H100; `base` = the unmodified model with full prefill): | dataset | n | metric | base | TokenGate (no pruning) | TokenGate @K=2000 | TTFT speedup @K=2000 | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | NIAH (16k) | 150 | acc | 0.993 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 6.3× | | RepoBench-P | 450 | ES | 0.285 | 0.587 | 0.550 | 3.8× | | BioDEX-Reactions | 450 | F1 | 0.056 | 0.284 | 0.292 | 2.1× | Tighter budgets trade little: NIAH stays at 1.000 acc down to K=100 (8.1×), RepoBench holds 0.533 ES at K=500 (5.6×). The no-pruning arm doubles as the fine-tuning reference — its gap to `base` is what the task-trained gate+adapter add. The TTFT gap widens with context length (the paper's 1.4–11.3× range comes from the longer-context tiers). The 50-row `val` partitions reproduce the same ordering (e.g. RepoBench 0.576/0.559, BioDEX 0.377/0.368 unpruned/@K=2000). Released checkpoints: the benchmark set above plus `liana313/tokengate-2wikimqa-qwen3-1.7b`, `liana313/tokengate-multinews-qwen3-1.7b`, and the hybrid-attention `liana313/tokengate-niah-qwen3.5-2b` — each repo holds the exact gate+LoRA checkpoint the paper's benchmarks used. ### Training the TokenGate model The released checkpoints train from the lane configs under `train-scripts/` (one script per dataset, gate layer 1 — each sets every hyperparameter of its run and calls the shared driver). Install with the `train` extras (see [Installation](#-installation)); the shell drivers read the interpreter from `PYTHON` — point it at your venv (`export PYTHON=$PWD/.venv/bin/python`) — and log to W&B (`wandb login`, or `WANDB_MODE=disabled`). The trainer reads pre-prepped tokenized stores. For BioDEX-Reactions (the official splits of [BioDEX](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BioDEX/BioDEX-Reactions), ~11.5k train articles): ```bash # one-time download of the official dataset into the HF cache python -c "import datasets; datasets.load_dataset('BioDEX/BioDEX-Reactions')" # tokenize into {train,val}.pkl for the base model python datasets/biodex/biodex_reactions/prepare.py # train (the packed memory-mapped token store is built automatically at launch) WANDB_PROJECT= bash train-scripts/example/run_e2e_gate_biodexr_example.sh ``` Common overrides (environment variables; see the script for the full list): ```bash NUM_GPUS=1 bash train-scripts/example/run_e2e_gate_biodexr_example.sh # single GPU MAX_STEPS=50 bash train-scripts/example/run_e2e_gate_biodexr_example.sh # smoke run ``` Outputs land under `e2e_gates///baseline/L/`: `gate_final.pt` + `lora_final.pt` (and SWA variants), periodic resumable checkpoints, `params.json`, and training-curve CSVs/plots. During training the model is evaluated every `EVAL_FREQ` steps on the pinned val split and the reserved held-out test split, at each K in `K_EVAL_VALUES`, alongside no-compression and random-selection reference baselines. The released demo checkpoint was trained with exactly this config. (For a synthetic dataset with no external download, see the NIAH lanes: `datasets/niah_kamradt/generate_niah_kamradt.py`.) ## 📚 Datasets Each dataset is a directory `datasets///` with a `prepare.py` that emits rows of `{article (the state), answer, id, metadata}` and tokenizes them into `tokenized//{train,val}.pkl`. A training run pins its dataset through a YAML manifest (`tokengate/datasets/manifests/iso_.yaml`) and pins its val/test split through an eval-split manifest — the explicit source of eval-set sizes. Scoring lives in `tokengate/datasets/tasks/` (one `Task` class per task: prompt format, metric, judge config). ## 📄 Citation If you find TokenGate useful, please cite our [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26754) ```bibtex @article{patel2026tokengate, title={TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning}, author={Patel, Liana and Ranjan, Rishabh and Stoica, Ion and Zaharia, Matei and Guestrin, Carlos}, journal={arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.26754}, year={2026} } ```

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "tokengate"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "TokenGate: The Missing Module For Fast And Memory-Efficient Prefill In LLMs"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.10"
license = { text = "Apache-2.0" }
dependencies = [
    "torch>=2.9",
    "transformers>=5.5,<6",
    "accelerate>=1.2",
    "datasets>=2.18.0",
    "huggingface-hub>=0.24",
    "numpy>=2.0",
    "tqdm>=4.66",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
    "safetensors>=0.4.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
# Training-run logging + curve plots (the trainer runs without them).
train = ["wandb>=0.16", "matplotlib>=3.8"]
# Metrics + data prep for specific datasets.
data = ["rouge-score>=0.1.2", "pyarrow>=15.0"]

[project.urls]
Repository = "https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["tokengate"]
# Manifests, eval splits and sampling maps ship with the package (the code
# resolves them relative to tokengate/datasets/).
artifacts = [
    "tokengate/datasets/manifests/*.yaml",
    "tokengate/datasets/eval_splits/*.json",
    "tokengate/datasets/maps/*.yaml",
]
